We saw it in Nice, at the 3rd UN Ocean Conference. Where governments committed to expand marine protected areas and tackle plastic pollution and illegal fishing. And we saw it in Sevilla, at the 4th International Financing for Development Conference, where countries agreed on a new vision for global finance— one that expands fiscal space, lowers the cost of capital, and ensures developing countries have a stronger voice and participation in the organizations that shape their future. These are not isolated wins. They are signs of momentum. Signs that multilateralism can deliver. Signs that transformation is not only necessary, it is possible. And that is the spirit we bring to this High-Level Political Forum. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, this Forum is about renewing our common promise to end poverty, protect the planet, and ensure prosperity for all. We also recognize the deep linkages between development and peace. We meet against the backdrop of global conflicts that are pushing the Sustainable Development Goals further out of reach. That is why we must keep working for peace in the Middle East. Over the weekend in Gaza, we saw yet more mass shootings and killings of people seeking UN aid for their families— an atrocious and inhumane act which I utterly condemn. We need an immediate ceasefire in Gaza. the immediate release of all hostages and unimpeded humanitarian access as a first step to achieve the two-state solution. We need the ceasefire between Iran and Israel to hold. We need a just and lasting peace in Ukraine, based in the UN Charter, international law, and UN resolutions. We need an end to the horror and bloodshed in Sudan. And the list goes on, from the DRC to Somalia, from the Sahel to Myanmar. At every step, we know sustainable peace requires sustainable development. The Sustainable Development Goals are not a dream. They are a plan. A plan to keep our promises— to the most vulnerable people, to each other, and to future generations. People win when we channel our energy into development. Since 2015, millions more people have access to electricity, clean cooking and the internet. Social protection now reaches over half the world's population— up from just a quarter a decade ago. More girls are completing school. Child marriage is declining. Women's representation is growing, from the boardrooms of business to the halls of political power. But we must face a tough reality: only 35% of SDG targets are on track or making moderate progress. Nearly half are moving too slowly, and 18% are going backwards. Meanwhile, the global economy is slowing. Trade tensions are rising. Inequalities are growing. Aid budgets are being decimated while military spending soars. And mistrust, division and outright conflicts are placing international problem-solving systems under unprecedented strain. We cannot sugarcoat those facts. But we must not surrender to them either. The SDGs still are within reach, if we act with urgency and ambition. This year's Forum focuses on 5 critical goals: health, gender equality, decent work, life below water, and global partnership. All are essential. All are interconnected. All can spur change across other goals. On health, COVID-19 exposed and deepened inequalities, and today far too many people still lack access to basic care. We know what works. We must boost investment in universal health coverage, rooted in strong primary care and prevention, reaching those furthest behind first. On gender equality, gaps remain wide. Women and girls face systemic barriers— from violence and discrimination to unpaid care and limited political voice. But we also see growing momentum— from grassroots movements to national reforms. Now is the time to turn that momentum into transformation. With rights-based policies, accountability, and real financing into programmes that support inclusion and equality for women and girls. On decent work, the global economy is leaving billions behind. Over 2 billion people are in informal jobs, and youth unemployment is stubbornly high. But we have tools to change these. The Global Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection is helping countries invest in expanded social protection initiatives, skills training and the creation of sustainable livelihoods, including in growing industries like clean energy. Tomorrow, I will deliver an address on the enormous opportunities of the renewables revolution. And the upcoming World Summit on Social Development can help spur further progress. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, on life below water, our ocean and the communities that count on it are paying the price of overfishing, pollution and climate change. We must deliver on the commitments of the Nice Ocean Conference to protect marine ecosystems and support the millions who depend on them. And finally, on global partnerships— SG17— we need to strengthen all the elements that can support progress. And this means investing in science, data and local capacity. And harnessing digital innovation, including artificial intelligence, to accelerate progress, not deepen divides. Throughout, we must recognize the need to reform the unfair global financial system, which no longer represents today's world or the challenges faced by developing countries. We must ensure a reform for developing countries to have a stronger voice and greater participation to help advance the Sustainable Development Goals on the ground. The Sevilla Commitments that emerged from the Conference on Financing for Development include important steps: through new domestic and global commitments that can channel public and private finance to the areas of greatest need; by increasing the capacity of governments to substantially mobilize domestic resources, including through tax reform; And by establishing a more effective framework for debt relief and tripling the lending capacity of multilateral development banks to the benefit of developing countries. Excellencies—

Excellencies, in the coming year, we must keep building. We must strengthen and scale up partnerships that deliver. Including with the private sector and civil society organizations and local authorities. We must embed long-term thinking into every decision, as we committed to in the Declaration on Future Generations, and we must continue to learn from each other. The group urges greater action to conserve and sustainably use the ocean, seas, and marine resources for sustainable development. We also stress the importance of enhancing the means of the full implementation of the BBNJ agreement. And capacity building in this regard. Mr. President, the group calls for the international community to seize the remaining years to 2030 to reshape global systems in ways that enable rather than constrain the development of the Global South. Development is a right, not a privilege. Let us recommit to building a more just inclusive and sustainable world for present and future generations. Our time to act is now. Thank you.

The 2024 July-August mass uprising in our country marked a historic reclamation of democracy and human rights, followed by a bold reform agenda to rebuild public trust, restore accountability, and embed justice at the heart of governance. Our people's aspirations have evolved for the better, and so has the nature of our engagement with the UN. Bangladesh is now proactively contributing to global norm-setting, instead of merely reacting to it. Our 3rd VNR presentation last week reflects this renewed ethos. It sets a higher bar for inclusivity and localization, bringing previously unheard voices into national policy pathways. Mr. President, our political and economic reforms coincide with our efforts to navigate the challenges posed by our LDC. We call for enhanced multilateralism and urge the international community to support our systemic transition through tailored measures and a staggered withdrawal of LDC-specific benefits. We need cooperation in fighting illicit financial flows, recovering stolen assets, and ensuring debt sustainability. The outcome of the recently concluded FFD4 gives us hope but past experiences also cause worries. We call for genuine political will to translate these ambitions into concrete outcomes. Mr. President, in its 80 years, with many accomplishments as well as unfinished promises, the UN remains a beacon of hope. Our shared progress reaffirms that multilateralism is not only relevant, it is our last resort. Let us harness our collective ambitions for SDGs and resolve to reshape a world of 3 zeros: zero poverty, zero unemployment, and zero net carbon emissions, espoused by our honorable chief advisor, Professor Muhammad Yunus, Nobel Peace Laureate. I thank you all.

I thank Mr. Chowdhury very much for his presentation. I now give the floor to Her Excellency Excellency Tatjana Makura, the Minister without Portfolio of Serbia, who shares a responsibility for the coordination of activities in the field of gender equality, prevention of violence against women, and economic and political empowerment of women. Minister, you're welcome.

Thank you, Mr. Chair, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. I would express my gratitude for this shared opportunity to discuss the topics of gender equality in the age of digitalization and artificial intelligence. Serbia is witnessing concrete progress in both of these areas. In the last decade, our country has made important strides in fostering economic growth and employment and lowering the risk of poverty. Serbia had one of the highest economic growth rates in Europe last year, measuring 3. Therefore, it should not surprise us that the participation of women in small businesses in Serbia is over 30% and that we have over 52% of female scientists. Keeping pace with technological development, we are also opening the conversation on gender equality in the digital, digital sphere. No progress is sustainable if it carries old injustice within it. That is why Serbia has initiated the development of ethical guidelines for the design and use of trustworthy artificial intelligence. We cannot allow that digital future to trap women between technological innovation and social tradition. Our experience tells us that sustainable solutions are built through partnerships. We cooperate with the United Nations, civil society, and the private sector. And we call on other countries to join us in advancing gender-responsive innovations, expecting good practices, exchanging good practices, and tracking progress. I am pleased to announce that Serbia, through the process of developing digital services and e-government, will open the e-woman platform as a unique one-stop shop for all information of importance to women: healthcare, maternity leave, opportunities for starting a business, violence prevention. In this sense, I believe it is also important to inform you, since the ratification of the Istanbul Convention and the adoption of the Law on the Prevention of Domestic Violence, our country has seen a steady decrease in the number of victims. victims. We are now at the historically lowest point in terms of number of victims. And our efforts do not stop here. By the end of this year, we expect amendments to the law on domestic violence and other related legislation, all with the aim of securing a safer and better life for every woman and girl. When you set gender equality as your goal, you inevitably touch on issues of health, education, economic inclusion, access to resources, and political participation. This topic is the foundation of all social progress, and if we succeed in achieving this one goal, we will accelerate progress on all the others. Thank you.

Thank you, Minister. Now I'll give the floor to His Excellency Fabrián Alfianto Rudyard, the Vice Minister of National Development Planning of Indonesia, on behalf of a group, the Alliance of Countries on the Fight Against Tuberculosis. His Excellency Mr. Rudyard will be the last speaker before we adjourn for lunch. Thank you, Mr. Secretary-General.

Mr. President, distinguished delegates, I'm delivering this statement on behalf of the Alliance of Countries on the Fight Against Tuberculosis. We commend the President of ECOSOC for his leadership in convening the 2025 High-Level Political Forum. Mr. President, tuberculosis remains one of the greatest challenges. For over a century, it has affected billions of lives, making it top infectious disease killer globally. In 2023 alone, over 10.8 million individuals developed TB and 1.25 million lost their lives. More than statistics, they represent lives impacted, families burdened, and communities affected. Despite the scale and gravity, global TB response continues to suffer from inadequate and unsustainable financing and insufficient prioritization. The Alliance reaffirmed its commitment to the 2023 Political Declaration on the Fight Against Tuberculosis. It constitutes an important roadmap for action, the most ambitious target to date, aiming to accelerate action by the next UN high-level meeting in 2028. TB must no longer be treated, as a disease of the past, but a present threat that requires urgent and coordinated action. We therefore call for the highest commitment to scale-up action, financing, and cooperation in the fight against TB, including multidrug-resistant TB. We welcome commitment expressed in this year's Ministerial Declaration and strongly call for its implementation, especially in addressing TB and other communicable diseases that continue to threaten development gains. Allow me to deliver a statement in my national capacity. Excellency, distinguished delegates, Indonesia comes to this forum with a strong commitment and renewed optimism. As the United Nations turns 80, we face a clear task to restore trust in multilateralism. In the face of global challenges, from war and climate crisis to inequality and hunger, we must ensure multilateralism works. That means reforms that are bold and focused. The Pact for the Future gives us a helpful direction, but to succeed, our system must be fit for purpose and future-ready. Indonesia offers 4 key actions to accelerate sustainable development. First, we need to unlock real change. That begins with equity. Leaving no one behind, Indonesia is pushing inclusive policies. Today, 98.8% of our people are covered by social health insurance and expanded social protection. We nearly ended extreme poverty. Second, we must scale up game-changing solutions that combine growth with sustainability. Indonesia's Blue Economy strategy protects marine life, supports coastal communities, and grows our economy. We also support digital transformation for MSMEs, especially those led by women, expanding access to digital markets and building resilience. Third, strong partnerships are essential. We need all hands on deck— government, businesses, civil society— sharing ideas, resources, and solutions. Indonesia promotes blended finance for SDGs and expands South-South and triangular cooperation to encourage mutual learning among developing countries. Our 4th Voluntary National Review reflects this spirit— learning from others and sharing our experience. Finally, we must act urgently and together. With just 5 years left to 2030, we cannot afford delay. We need global solidarity that restores trust, strengthens cooperation, and puts sustainability at the core of all we do. Indonesia is ready to act, to partner, and to lead, because the future we dream of depends on what we do starting today. Let me close with a humble verse. Across blue seas, sails glide with grace. Together we move one shared space. The SDGs are more than just a goal. They are the heart, the guide, and the soul. I thank you, Mr. President.
Thank you.

I thank the distinguished delegate. I think he left us on a very good note with which to conclude today's session, that the SDGs are not just a goal, they are also our heart and soul. I think we can all agree with that and thank him very much for that comment. Colleagues, we've just heard the last speaker for This meeting. The general debate will continue at 3 PM, but not here.
